processing: Oxidised less than other Wuyi rock teas (one seller puts it at 25 to 50 percent) and usually roasted only lightly, because its tender pale leaves scorch easily; the gentlest-made of the classic Wuyi bushes.
harvest_season: One spring picking, late April to early May; the pale yellow-green shoots are picked a little younger than for other rock teas.
appearance_dry: Loosely twisted strips in yellow-olive and tan, visibly paler than any other rock tea.
appearance_liquor: Pale gold to light amber, bright.
appearance_wet: Soft, thin, yellowish leaves with a faint red rim; the lightest-coloured wet leaf in the Wuyi range.
taste_profile: Soft and sweet rather than roasted: honeyed hay, fresh pear, mild herbs and a light sourness like a good white tea, with a cooling finish and only a whisper of mineral grip.

brewing.notes: Porcelain gaiwan, water just off the boil. Keep the leaf ratio a little lower than for heavy yancha and the steeps short; this is a delicate tea and heavy handling only makes it thin and sour.

vintage_note: Spring harvest of the current year, lightly roasted in early summer and sold from late summer or autumn with the year stated. Because the roast is light it is a drink-young tea: best within a year or two of harvest, kept sealed, and not a candidate for ageing or re-roasting.
description:
Bai Ji Guan is the odd one out among the four famous bushes of Wuyi: where Tie Luo Han and Shui Jin Gui are dark and roasted, this one is pale, soft and almost white-tea-like. The name means white cockscomb and describes the plant, whose young shoots are a whitish yellow-green with downy, slightly curled tips.

The pale colour is a natural trait of the cultivar, which is low in chlorophyll, and it dictates how the tea is made. The leaves cannot take the heavy shaking and charcoal roasting of ordinary yancha without going flat and sour, so makers oxidise them lightly and give them a light roast, just enough to dry and settle them. The result is a rock tea that keeps its yellow colour, its honeyed, hay-like sweetness and a gentle fruitiness that most drinkers compare to pear or dried apricot.

Tradition places the mother bushes in the core scenic zone, either below Huoyan Peak in the Hui Yuan Yan area or behind the Wen Gong temple at Wuyi Palace, depending on which account you read, and the cultivar has always been scarce because it yields poorly and grows slowly. It was propagated by cuttings in the twentieth century and is now grown in small quantities around the mountain, mostly for the curiosity market and for sets of the four famous bushes.

In the cup it starts light and floral-sweet, picks up a soft herbal note and a faint cooling sourness in the middle steeps, and fades politely. It does not have the throat-coating mineral weight of a Rou Gui and it is a mistake to brew it looking for one; use water just off the boil, slightly less leaf, and short steeps, and drink it on its own rather than after a heavy tea.

It is sold by the current spring harvest, and freshness matters: a Bai Ji Guan that has sat for three years in a shop drawer tastes of nothing. Buy small amounts from a seller who states the year, and keep it sealed. If you enjoy the light-roast side of Wuyi, Huang Guan Yin and lightly roasted Qi Lan are the logical next steps.
sources_note: Two traditional origin accounts exist (Hui Yuan Yan below Huoyan Peak, and the Wen Gong temple at Wuyi Palace); both are given as tradition. The low-chlorophyll description of the cultivar is from Chinese cultivar literature.
history:
Bai Ji Guan is one of the four famous bushes of Wuyi. One Chinese overview says it was already highly regarded in the late Ming and early Qing, before Da Hong Pao made its name, and a tea seller's article places the name in the Ming as well, though neither cites an early record. Two places are given for the original bush: under Huoyan Peak at Hui Yuan Yan, or at the Wen Gong shrine at Wuyi Palace.

The legends are more colourful than the record. One says a monk buried a rooster that died defending its chick from an eagle, and the bush grew from that spot. Another says a Ming prefect's sick son was cured by a cup of it at Wuyi Palace, and the tea went on to the emperor.

The solid part is the plant. Bai Ji Guan is a yellow-leaf cultivar, which sets it apart from the darker Wuyi bushes, and Chinese breeders have used it as a parent for the newer yellow-leaf variety Zhongcha 211.
